utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Monday, May 25th. I would like to greet Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Pusic. I also greet the Defence counsel. I greet Mr. Stringer and everyone helping him, and I also greet our court reporter and the interpreters, registrar, as well as the usher. We have a short oral decision to render, and you will read it immediately. Oral decision on the request by Prosecution and the accused Praljak for a stay of the proceedings. On May 8, 2009, Prosecution requested a stay in the proceedings for three days for June, 9, 10 and 11, 2009. On May 21st, 2009, the counsels of accused Praljak also requested a stay in the proceedings for the same dates. No objection was raised by the other parties, and, therefore, the Trial Chamber decides to grant these motions and to stay the proceedings on June 9, 10, and 11, 2009. There will be no hearings for those three days on June 9, 10, and 11. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to express my appreciation to the Trial Chamber and all the parties for their understanding on this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stringer. The hearing will now resume, and we will continue with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Praljak, and so I give the floor to Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to you and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we resume, I'd like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the following: With respect to document 3D0 -- no, not document, video 3D03114, which was the video showing the events in Travnik with members of the HVO who had left the front line, the Defence checked the video, listened to it again, checked the translation, and we claim that the interpretation into English is correct and translates precisely the words that General Praljak uttered. So that's what I'd say -- I'd like to say about that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, General. What was it you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, I did not say -- or say the words that you were translated -- that were translated that we would fuck Imater [phoen] and so on. I used a very neutral form, a neutral word, "Jebemumate [phoen]," or "fuck you." So it has nothing to do with the question you raised about what had been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is noted. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, on Thursday we left off discussing the events in Gornji Vakuf of the 18th of January and moving on slowly to the 19th, and you spoke about your attempts to come into contact with General Petkovic, who at that time was in Geneva. So would you continue from that point, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I arrived on the 16th and that the Deputy Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO at the time, Andric, and the commander of the area of responsibility, Mr. Siljeg, had had a series of contacts with the opposite side; and I said that the BH Army had taken up positions in the town of Vakuf, quite simply in and around Vakuf. Well, that's what I was told. And I knew that from before, from December 1992, in fact. That the Serb lines were about 10 kilometres as the crow flies from Radusa Kamen, and that for various reasons the conflict had already begun on the 11th of January, 1993. After we had those discussions and we saw that the HVO -- what the HVO proposals were and that they had consulted me, of course, and that they were very reasonable and precise and, militarily speaking, okay and correct, in order to achieve some sort of agreement for a cease-fire to be put in place I came into contact with Geneva. Well, not directly. I wasn't able to contact Geneva directly but had to go through Gojko Susak's secretary or some such round about route. That's how I did it, I assume. And I think Sefer Halilovic was up there as well. So I asked that they agree and send an official order for a cease-fire. What happened up there was this: Every time the HVO stopped, according to the information that I was conveyed by Andric and Siljeg, the BH Army continued to fight using sniper fire. They carried on killing and wounding people, and they showed no signs of resolving the situation in a peaceful way. The HVO achieved military success there. That is to say it took control of the surrounding hills but with a lot of casualties and fatalities. Lots died and were wounded. And on the 20th of January, I think, an order arrived for a cease-fire. And in situations like that, to effect a cease-fire is a slow process. You can't stop straight away, because the military situation is such that it requires a gradual easing. It has to reach the commanders in the field. Their communications are down, but anyway, Andric and Siljeg did their best. However, I should also like to mention that with -- according to all my information, in Gornji Vakuf it wasn't actually possible, because you had that man, Paraga, up there, who was a renegade from the BH Army and some other people who were in the army of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the civilian structures of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just to avoid any misunderstanding, Paraga is the nickname of who?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prijic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer to your question who is Paraga is not at all reflected in the record. I haven't actually heard it either. Perhaps you were overlapping. So perhaps you ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, who is Paraga, or who last Paraga?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a -- the nickname of a person called Hanefija Prijic. It was a unit that was completely out of control, which had killed three Italians from the humanitarian -- or, rather, humanitarian workers, and he was of the people who behaved in this way in the BH Army. So what I can say in conclusion is this: With major losses, the HVO, on the basis of everything I knew of a purely military action, succeeded to deblock, to completely lift the blockade of the roads and HVO units and the commands. And on the 22nd of January, I had the task of following the order from Mr. Petkovic preventing the town from being taken over; and I claim that the HVO, at that point in time, by virtue of its position and strength, was able to take the town of Uskoplje. And I claim once again that that was not the intention or wish. We did not want to have a conflict with the BH Army beyond not allowing them to set up a complete -- blockade of the HVO in Gornji Vakuf tantamount to an aggression in military terms. That is an aggression. Now, a response to that aggression is called active defence, and so on the 22nd, I told the commanders, and -- I told them why I was asked to go there, pursuant to General Petkovic's orders. I said no, the town will remain free and peace is going to be restored. Now, to restore peace after you've just been at war is a difficult thing. On the 23rd, in the morning, I returned to Mostar, and that completes my role as far as Uskoplje was concerned and the events there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, for the record and for the benefit of everybody in the courtroom, document 3D00476, which is already an exhibit and was admitted by the Trial Chamber, is a document which testifies to the number of killed and wounded in the Gornji Vakuf operation. So we won't take up more time with that, but it is to be found in the document which is already an exhibit. General, we decided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I listened to your version of the events, the versions you gave us of the events as of January 20th, and I must tell you that I can't understand. Why is it -- I can't understand, because on January 15th there was an important meeting in Zagreb attended by all major -- all major players, Mate Boban, Tudjman, Izetbegovic, Cyrus Vance, Lord Owen, and this meeting obviously had an objective to restore peace, restoring a cease-fire and bringing calm to the environment; and then you're telling us that in a unit that was out of control, Paraga's unit, is on the field, is operating on the field, and you as HVO in the framework of the concept of active defence, and these are the words that you actually used, "active defence," you managed to lift the blockade of the roads and to control hills -- the hills. This is exactly what you said, and I can't understand what actually happened. If this Mr. Paraga is out of control and suddenly starts operating while not following what had been decided in Zagreb, why didn't the HVO, through Mr. Boban, decide to directly call upon Mr. Izetbegovic, as well as Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen and Tudjman, to say, We have a problem. We have an eye BiH unit that is totally out of control and is totally disturbing the environment. And then there could be a joint action that could have been decided, but obviously you didn't choose to embark on that route. You decided to go along active defence, and this is where I run into a problem here. So what can you say to this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, the problem of Paraga is just one that was prominent. However, the leadership in Gornji Vakuf as well, and the commanders of the BH Army in Gornji Vakuf, and the commanders of the 3rd Corps of the BH Army to which that area belonged, in those hills spent three months digging, three months before this event. A whole series of meetings in December took place, as I've already said here once, and it was under pressure from me and my instructions that Mr. Andric and Mr. Siljeg discuss this with the opposite side in treating them and warning them that a friendly army or a joint army or some sort of army that was supposed to act together didn't behave in that way. It wasn't done. It was preparation for complete control of the roads going into Central Bosnia, and that it was tantamount to placing the HVO in Gornji Vakuf under complete control. I also said that the commander of the HVO brigade from Vakuf and Uskoplje, Tokic was his name, was not able to reach his headquarters and command. For example, going from Rama, going from Rama, he had to ask UNPROFOR to transport him, and as we saw when we looked at the map and as a British officer demonstrated, at all the elevations, both in town and around town, they had dug trenches. They had been fortifying themselves for months. And you saw these trenches on the photographs as well, photographs which were taken last year or the year before, and you can still see that it was no improvisation. So faced with a situation of this kind, it wasn't only Paraga who acted as he did, but there was quite a different line of thought in whole sections of the BH Army, and the commanders of the BH Army, and I don't know who else as well, because something like that cannot be done. You can't do something like that without others knowing or receiving permission from the higher-ranking officers from those who were in Gornji Vakuf, especially as throughout December the BH Army was being asked to do away with the trenches and the HVO blockades of the roads leading into Central Bosnia. For example, in Bugojno at the time, everything was quiet. There were no problems there. So it was not just Paraga. Paraga was just an extreme example. This was a military action to block the -- what was supposed to be a partner army, especially since by the 11th they already left all the lines leading -- or facing the Serbs, Republika Srpska army, and the HVO then had to man to prevent any break-through -- their break-through towards Vakuf. Now, whether Mr. Izetbegovic knew that in Zagreb, whether he knew everything, I don't know that, but when I was asked to go down there, I told him some of it, because by forcing, so to speak, Siljeg and Andric to talk and to negotiate and try to resolve it peacefully, in November I knew that it was a big part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this is a lengthy answer, but in diplomatic terms, it's not complete. You are noting what is happening military-wise on the field, and you told us about it. You told us that they dug trenches and so forth and so on. You also note that they have no intention of entering into the diplomatic game that was set up in Zagreb. Very well, but why don't you report to Mate Boban telling him, This is the situation. What should I do? Should I attack them in the framework of active defence, or should you, Mr. Boban, call Mr. Izetbegovic, Lord Owen, and all of them, to tell them about the situation, tell hem that there is a problem? When you decided to act militarily, did you get the green light, or did you do this on your own volition, if I could say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Antonetti, my answers are long because it always seem to me that my role is not understood properly here. The commanders in the field have the right to decide on many issues. So the deputy chief of the Main Staff and the commander of the operational zone, they have responsibility vis-a-vis their troops, the troops under their commander. And on the 11th of January, they started conflicts with the BH Army. On the 15th of January, I was asked to go down there and to calm things down, and I entered the story on the 16th of January. By that time those guys had already gone to Geneva, and I'm in the field. Our communications -- well, I could -- I find it really hard to get in touch with Geneva from Rama, from Prozor. And immediately on the 16th Siljeg and Andric were sent again to -- for another round of talks in Vakuf. All the documents are here. I don't want to go through them again. And there the demands before them were very clear, because demands were made in the army that military should withdraw from Vakuf, that no rifles are carried by the troops, that the joint police should be set up, the joint check-points should be set up, and so on and so forth. And all the things that I suggested should be placed as demands, I still stand by it. It is logical, and it is justified in military terms. So I supported two of the HVO commanders in their logical demands. And now since the other side turned a deaf ear and every time there was a cease-fire they would fire on people, they would kill people. They had casualties. And at the same time I had this parallel situation. I informed Petkovic about what was going on because he was the chief of the Main Staff, and at the same time he has his deputy and the zone commander, and they are responsible vis-à-vis their troops; and the responsibility is not to let them become casualties and not to let them be encircled or blocked totally, because when the cease-fire was signed and you could see from the documents that were here the destruction of the trenches took months and with UNPROFOR controlling the whole operation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let me stop you here. I fully understand -- understood that you're saying, but there's something that just doesn't work, doesn't click. And there's everything -- there's a very complicated architecture that's set up. We have General Petkovic in Geneva with Halilovic, but you on the field, you observe the situation because the enemy, "ABiH", is playing its own game according to you; and you decide to trigger an attack, call it active defence or defensive, defence, whatever. There is a conflict when everybody, on the other hand, is trying to cool things down. So this is what I can't reconcile. According to your answer, I feel that while apprehending the situation on the ground, you decide -- you made a military decision without taking the diplomatic negotiations into account. You decided to go against the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think you're wrong, Your Honour. In military terms, yes. If -- let's assume -- let me take the liberty to assume. Let's say we are partners in something. Then you will not let me train my machine-gun at you and to control where you go and how you go about. So the diplomatic efforts and everything that was going on, there was always this element, please don't keep your machine-gun trained on me, because in military terms this is inadmissible. So peace the way they saw it according to the documents that you have, resulted in dozens of casualties in HVO ranks. My duty was to prevent the conflict from escalating and not to take the town at any cost because that was not the intention. But if somebody controls every step that's taken in Vakuf and controls seven or eight main positions, key positions, and I drew them very accurately on the map and this English major testified about them here very accurately, they simply had a situation where they could shoot and kill people at will, and there was always an incident. So if you have three dead one day, it's an incident. Four killed the other day, it's an incident. Five killed the day after, again an incident. Then the commanders have an obligation. Nobody sent an order from Geneva that the commanders of the partner armies should behave in the way that we proposed, that everybody should move out of the town, pull out to the lines facing the Republika Srpska army. So this was a response to a conflict that they had caused two months before, and it resulted in a great number of casualties, a number of killed and wounded soldiers of the HVO. And I'm afraid that Mr. Izetbegovic did not have any control over those units, and when I get to the books, I will show how the BH Army actually functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your lengthy answer. Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I would like to ask you to take the Gornji Vakuf file which is to your left. We will have to have to go through some of the documents in order to show the situation. Now I would like to ask you if you could look at P01114. Well, you can look at the screen in e-court. There won't be that many documents. This is the Main Staff of the HVO. The date is the 13th of January, 1993. P01114. I would like to draw your attention only to Gornji Vakuf. You have it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Gornji Vakuf. It's a summary report on events in the area of Gornji Vakuf, and the date is the 13th of January. And in this document there is a mention about the possibility that the conflict might occur, and the events of the 13th of January. You were not there at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I was told about that. I was in the field until Christmas throughout December, and I know what it means to provoke conflicts on a daily basis, on a daily basis, and putting the other side in a subordinate position, and this culminates and culminates; and it is completely understandable that the commanders on the opposite side cannot allow this mistreatment, because this is what it amounted to, abuse, maltreatment, killing people, wounding people, and in effect --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I would like us to look at 3D0153 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I like to ask a question of you, Mr. Praljak. Here in this report, one of the first incidents mentioned culminating and culminating in lowering the Croatian flag. Now, where was the Croatian flag lowered, and what was the legal basis for the Croatian flag having been drawn up? If you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I -- I know about the incident. This is described in an earlier event. I know partially. I don't know exactly. There was a building where the HVO was. It was on this building, and I think that it was for Christmas that the BH Army set the flag on fire, tore it up, and of course -- well, why was it flown at all? Because, Your Honour, we are a constituent people in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we had the right to display our historical emblem and the flag, as did the BH Army, because the flag that they adopted was not recognised as the flag of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was changed later. It was the flag with the Fleur-de-lis emblem which they considered, and of course they used flags with crescent moon. In fact, 50 percent of their units carried flags that had the insignia associated with Islamic religion. Simply, in the war armies carrying flags, and the Croats, without wishing to impose their solution on anyone flew their historical flag on the buildings that they used, not the flag that meant that they had any aspirations to anything but as a people that has the right to be treated equally with all the -- with the other two peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this incident with the burning of the flag is very sensitive. If flags are being burnt, that means that the situation is very bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: On the other hand, Mr. Praljak, may not the other side have a different view and regard it as possibly under certain circumstances a provocation if the flag is raised? For instance, in a -- in a municipality which is inhabited predominantly by Muslims? Could they not have a different view which might be balanced against the Croatian view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, of course their position was different, but this position shows that they did not recognise Croats as a people with equal rights within the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the problem, because by and large the politicians and the personnel in the BH Army thought that they would dominate Bosnia and Herzegovina the way that Serbs dominated Yugoslavia. I would never allow, and I don't know of any instance when the HVO -- well, apart from the lunatics in Rama and so on, that I fought with using pistols, that anyone allowed the flag of another people to be trampled on. They, Muslims, had the right to deploy their own flags. Serbs had their flag and Croats had their own natural flag until it is determined, as it was after the war, what the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina should look like, and then it becomes obligatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the question of the flag lies at the heart of these incidents that have occurred on several occasions, but amongst intelligent and educated people, did nobody ever think of hoisting both flags at the top of a building, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, you have seen the photographs that I've shown here. In the war, initially the Croatian and the Muslim flag were tied together if you remember, as a sign of unity. I showed this Court those photographs. This is -- was the situation at the outset. But little by little, and I shall substantiate this by documents, if not today then tomorrow, slowly Sefer Halilovic and other people on their side started changing their positions. So you could see that Petkovic is a Ustasha, and they all are Ustashas down there. This was already obviously in 1990. Many of those people started thinking that Bosnia and Herzegovina was their own state, their domicile, and that the Croats and Serbs can go to their respective states, the Croats to Croatia. And that was the dominant idea, which was the prime mover of the ABiH Army's attack on the Croats, on the HVO throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. As far as the Croats are concerned, they thought that the Muslims could hoist their flag until the conflict flared up and escalated. After that time, things changed. And if you remember, the commander from Capljina, Luburic to whom I brought the insignias of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we actually gave them the patches with the lilies, with the Fleur-de-lis for them to wear on their uniforms. I personally did that. I did not bring them the Croatian coat of arms. I wanted them to bear insignia with their own emblems on their uniforms, and no one challenged that. So we did so until the end of 1992, and Luburic, too. That is something that I know for a fact. But Sefer Halilovic and some of his commander, and I will show this, this was impossible; for him, Petkovic and the entire HVO team were Ustashas already in 1990 in his view and even before, even while he was a member of the KOS, K-O-S, all the Croats were Ustashas to him. That is at the root much their attack on us because they thought themselves a fundamental nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if they are the fundamental nation, the basic nation, where does it put me? It puts me into a subordinate position, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Where does Mr. Sefer Halilovic come from?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic is not from Bosnia and Herzegovina. He came to Bosnia and Herzegovina as a citizen of Serbia and Sandzak. As an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army who worked for the counter-intelligence service, the KOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The transcript says Croatian flag?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is the historical flag of the Croatian people. The classical tricolour. It has identical colours, red, white, and blue as the flag of the Netherlands. Tricolour flag as many states have, and in the centre is the coat of arms, which has been the Croatian people's coat of arms for eight centuries, through the 25 red and white fields it symbolises the unification of north and southern Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But it is not the flag of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. General, the first sentence of this document reads: "From the Christmas holidays up-to-date, there was -- there -- since Christmas, the relationship between the HVO and the BH Army has become increasingly tense culminating in the lowering of the Croatian flags, bringing in of additional BH Army forces, setting up check-points in and around the town, so --" and it goes on to describe what happened. So it was not the Croatian flag that was actually the cause of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Croatian flag was not the cause of this. It was just one in a series of open, overt attacks, and the putting of a very important place under control. And in his book the American Colonel Shrader in his book about the war in Central Bosnia, and I have it in front of me, and I will show you. He claims that the army had planned the attack on Gornji Vakuf, that it had been planned in advance for strategic reasons so that later on he could operate unhindered in Central Bosnia, in Travnik, at other places without any help being able to arrive to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We still have to see 3D01537. It will be on the screen for your benefit, so you don't have to look for it. 3D01537. This is a document of the 1st of January, 1993. The readiness of units for use signed by Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic. I should like to ask you to take a look at this document and pay special attention to item 4 in it. Can you read it? Are you able to -- could the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see. I'm able to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: To take land features from which action was taken against our forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It always starts like this. If the HVO attacks us first. This is a false formulation which is always resorted to and which always puts the HVO in this thankless position. So if they should take action, then they should be smashed and as they say here the 3rd Brigade and 7th Brigade, Muslim brigades will be at full readiness with the battalion, et cetera. So the entire situation, the entire scenario has been prepared. This actually means that you provoke, provoke for so long, and in military terms to provoke means actually kill until you react, and when you do react, then I will say, Now you have attacked me; and then I will have taken advantage of that situation to take that area and subdue you. This is a classic scenario, perfidious military tactics where someone heckles you and riles you all the time and once when you say enough is enough, then this kind of a situation happens and this is what they were preparing for and this is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We only have another two documents and then we shall move on. P01216 is one. This is a document dated the 19th of January, 1993, signed by Colonel Zeljko Siljeg. It is a reply to the ultimatum of Senad Dautovic. Who was Senad Dautovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senad Dautovic was the commander of BH units in Bugojno, and in this letter Colonel Siljeg, the commander of the zone of operations in the area tells him, Dautovic, this is not what we looked for. We did not look for this, and you know very well who cooked this up, your side. It is not our wish to expand the conflict, for the conflict to escalate, but if it does, we will have to accept it. And he tells him, wherever you had a normal attitude and had reasonable people, there were never any problems from our side. And that is the case of Bugojno. In Bugojno there never were any problems, and the HVO actually allowed, because it was so unprepared, because it was complacent in its attitude towards the BH Army, it allowed itself to be routed sometime around July 1993, because they were lulled up. That was the tactics. They dug trenches in the city. They carried out all the necessary preparations. And the HVO, because it did not want in any way to actually deteriorate the situation, they were defeated in just one day. 15.000 people fled, and the Bugojno brigade, and there was total catastrophe. This is not to be done in the army. This is no way to act in the military. The army has weapons, and everyone has to know what they are to do, because those -- had not the people in Gornji Vakuf been ready and prepared, their fate would have been the same as those in -- the fate of -- the fate that befell the people of Bugojno. They say peace, peace, okay, and then the Muslim army prepares itself as we saw with Alagic, and with Bugojno and in Central Bosnia, and there you are, as we saw in Konjic, et cetera. So wherever they were even in the least -- where they had supremacist even in the least. And we were not prepared to clash with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were routed. We were defeated in a major way. But it is a fact, I repeat, we could have taken Vakuf, but obviously because this was prohibited it was not the intention of the HVO to have this conflict escalate, and the BH Army actually did so in Bugojno and in Vares and in Konjic and in Fojnica. They acted in precisely that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Document P01238, please. This is a document of the 20th of January, 1993, by now already an exhibit and a document that confirms exactly what we are talking about now. General Praljak, the document is from the commander of the 4th Corps of the BH Army, order. P01238. The Main Staff of the HVO and the BH Army staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This was already after the -- after General Petkovic had got into touch with Mostar down there and that is it. But look here, item 2, bullet 2: "From the municipality of Gornji Vakuf withdrawal all forces from the adjacent municipalities." This was also demanded in December. Also, the meeting on the 16th of January with UNPROFOR present. And on the 20th when they were defeated for the most part it was agreed to do so. This is a plea for units from the outside to move, because they were riotous. They were out of control -- no, not out of control. I'm not saying the right thing. They were under somebody's control, and these units in carrying out their intentions was under somebody's control. I don't know whose, but I know when I was there, and I was there in Rama, I know what was happening, and I was informed about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D02212. That is the next document. And as -- so 3D2212. This is an order by Colonel Zeljko Siljeg from the 22nd of January, 1992 [as interpreted], which reflects the behaviour -- shows the behaviour of the HVO in respect of the ordered or achieved cease-fire. I should like to direct you to item 3 and 5, items 3 and 5.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the commanders were particularly bothered by was the fact that the propaganda that one could hear on radio Sarajevo, et cetera; at that time, all this reported that mosques were being targeted, this and that was being done. So war propaganda, the propaganda of spreading lies, in fact. And they were particularly sensitive to that for the simple reason that the HVO did not have any counter-propaganda to speak of, although UNPROFOR was there, and they were able to see everything; but he's asking again the units and joining up on the units that they have to conduct themselves in keeping with the law of war, that they have to comply with orders. This was, of course, done orally very often in order to instill it upon every single man that the war had to be waged by means which are allowed in war. Until the 22nd, the time until which I was there, up there, I didn't see a single report that would demonstrate there had been any breaches of any rules of law, which does not, of course, mean that I had the correct information. I had information that I had, and that was the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter, I think it is January 1993, not January 1992, and is stated in the record. I think you misspoke. Page 21, line 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is 1993. I haven't been following the transcript, so I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, now we are done as far as Vakuf is concerned, but before we move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General, this last document signed by Colonel Siljeg, in paragraph 1 it seems that he is challenging the renegade elements in the ABiH. Is this a diplomatic formula to avoid the responsibility being borne by the ABiH for what happened, or is it something which colonel is noticing since he is responsible and in charge in the area, and he realises that part of the ABiH has violated everything that was being prepared in Geneva? If that is the case, why did Colonel Siljeg not ask for any sanctions? And in addition, why is there no copy of this order that was sent off to the cabinet of Mate Boban for information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, a copy of this document was most certainly sent to the Main Staff, and Mate Boban received summary reports. Secondly, this is not a diplomatic -- this is not diplomatic to the effect that the renegades had to be treated so-and-so. What we saw, Mr. Siljeg and all of us could see that there were two streams evolving in parallel in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina with one gaining prominence as time went by and the other one losing in importance. So the situation in the -- in the HVO, in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Mostar, was peaceful. In Konjic things functioned. In Jablanica they functioned. And some ten days before that I had left Central Bosnia where the situation was reasonably orderly. There was a satisfactory level of law and order, et cetera. But at that time in Bugojno, the situation was more than good. The level of cooperation was satisfactory. We had joint meetings. So Siljeg fails to understand, and he thinks that what was happening in Bosnia -- in Vakuf was being done by disaffected elements from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because there was nothing to be done with him except that they have put him in a totally disasters military situation in this brigade in Vakuf, and this is why this refers to this renegade situation or element.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, General, on Thursday we discussed the 15th of January, 1993, and the order issued both by Bruno Stojic and Milivoj Petkovic, and also Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and you gave us your explanation. However, you did mention that it was necessary to look at additional documents. So we provided a small file for Their Honours entitled "Additional documents." They are 2D01409, 2D00441, and P01343, and they are documents which relate to the 15th of January, 16th of January, and 20th of January, 1993. Just a moment I have to repeat the first number 2D01409. It is an order from Bozo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, this order was late by just one day, probably, because Bozo Rajic was not in Sarajevo but was somewhere else. Anyway, he was the minister of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on the basis of the agreement that I spoke about, he issued an order and this is what it is, referring to the three armies, although, in fact, it is unrealistic that he should issue an order of this kind to Mladic and so on. But anyway, negotiations had already started, so in view of the fact that they considered that Bosnia-Herzegovina was also what the territory occupied by the Army of Republika Srpska, that this is how it should be written, to see who wasn't going to respect the agreement reached if the negotiations on Bosnia-Herzegovina had been conducted and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we have a document here on the screen. Let me give the number again, because I believe it's very important. 2D01407 -- no, 1409. 2D01409. This is a document signed by Bozo Rajic. You told us that he's the minister of defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This document seems to go against what we had thought we understood when Mr. Okun testified. If I remember right, Mr. Okun seemed to hint that the HVO had anticipated the Geneva conference, but in this document we see, and it's written black -- in black and white, that all formations of the HVO in provinces 1, 5, and 9 will be under ABiH command; that all formations of ABiH in provinces 3, 8, and 10 will be under HVO command; and, most importantly, all formations of the Serbian army in provinces 2, 4, and 6 will be proclaimed to be Serbian provinces. Now, General Praljak, this is my question: On -- on your side it seems that as of January 15th, you asked for the ABiH units to be subordinated to you in provinces 3, 8, and 10. So isn't the -- this document the version for these provinces of what you asked for, provinces 1, 5 and 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Judge Antonetti, in Geneva some agreements had had already been signed, and one of them, as far as I remember, was the one that said that if more negotiations were going to be conducted on a proposed resolution by the international community, that while these negotiations are still going on, on a political level, that the war should stop so that the armies would not be in conflict with each other. It is more than logical for this kind of solution, a mirror-image solution, to be signed between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council. For example, you can command the HVO in these provinces, and we're going to command the BH Army in those provinces. Now, Your Honours, when you say that, it's not true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I agree with what you're saying. An agreement had been signed. But according to Mr. Okun, who was sitting in your chair just a few months ago, he seemed to say that you had implemented the agreement in anticipation, and if you had done this, you were not the only one, because the Muslim side seems to have done exactly the same thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was agreed with Alija Izetbegovic in Zagreb, the talks that I took part in, and I took part in the compiling of this document. I can't tell you more than that. This was a major attempt that had been made. Now, I can't go through all the documents. That would take up much -- too much time, but you have them. They are exhibits. It says without -- without pre-empting a political solution, okay, you decide what you want in Geneva, but until you have decided fully, let's stop the conflicts, and then you can negotiate peacefully and calmfully -- calmly. The HVO will respect every political solution made in Geneva. So nothing was foreseen here. This was an attempt to stop the war, and it was agreed upon with Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Susak. I think that also present at the negotiations was either Vance or Owen, Lord Owen, and that was signed by the defence minister, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic's minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, General Praljak, which means that for you, as of January 15th all this was supposed to be implemented on the ground, i.e., a single command for areas 3, 8, and 10, and 1, 5, and 9; 3, 8, and 10 were to be under HVO command, and 1, 5, and 9 under ABiH command. And there was no need for wait for weeks or months or anything. This was supposed to be implemented on the ground as of January 15th. Is this what we're supposed to understand; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, Judge. And apart from that, in these provinces, the HVO was subordinated to the BH Army straight away; and all the provinces that were called Muslim provinces here. But anyway, the HVO in those provinces was subordinated to the BH Army just as you heard say here, both in Tuzla, and Sarajevo, and Bihac, and so on and so forth. Unfortunately, the BH Army -- or, rather, Halilovic and the others never imagined that they would actually do something. They were the HVO. They had quite different plans and developments were quite different unfortunately, as I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I note something that seems important when the Judges will have to deliberate in order -- we need to have all this in mind. There are two elements on item 7. It says that the execution of this order will start as of January 20th at midnight, seemingly. And as recipients, we have also UNPROFOR and ECMM. So it seems that the international community is kept informed. UNPROFOR is recipient number 6. ECMM is recipient number 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We did hope, of course with UNPROFOR and the ECMM, that all of them would try to put this kind of order into practice. However, to be quite frank, many people weren't interested in stopping the war, in actual fact. And secondly, for this kind of order to be carry out, you need three or four days, and that's were Mr. Bozo Rajic says on the 20th of January was the date by way this should have been agreed because communications had to be established and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not on the field, but on January 20th, in provinces 3, 8, and 10, did you go and meet with your counterparts from the ABiH to tell them, Now we're in command. And did your officers in provinces 1, 5, and 9 meet with their Muslim counterparts to tell them, We are now under your command. Is this the way things happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first point of your conclusion, that is to say that had they done anything to set up a Joint Command in 3, 8, and 10 provinces, never entered their head. That's the first point. Secondly -- well, my answer is yes, in provinces 1, 6 [as interpreted], and 9, the HVO did place its self under the command the BH Army, and that was the situation until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have evidence proving this in 1, 5, and 9? There's a mistake in line 9. It's 1, 5 and not 6. Do you have any evidence proving that HVO officers actually placed themselves under ABiH command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you heard testimony here from the number one or -- number two or number three man from the Tuzla Corps whose units were there. You saw the situation around Sarajevo, how the HVO was under command -- what command the HVO was under and in Bihac the same. I can, of course, connect the documents, but they've been presented to this Court a number of times, both documents and testimony to accompany them. And I'm quite sure of that. I'm quite sure we have already presented them to the Trial Chamber along with the witnesses, the documents and the witnesses together; and they're saying what I'm saying, that in the provinces with the so-called Muslim majority the HVO was placed under the command of the BH Army to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as early as January 21st when you noted that in provinces 3, 8, and 10, it was not working. Did you -- did the -- was the information immediately fed back to political authorities, to Mr. Mate Boban, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, so they would know that there is a problem that the orders are not being carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of them. All the people you mentioned, every single one of them knew full well that we had been tricked in that respect and that the BH Army had absolutely no intention of subordinating themselves to -- in these province and to set up a joint commander with the HVO, and in that respect, you'll see far we participated. You will see the meetings in a Mr. Petkovic had with Sefer, the attempts that were made. However, they mined it all. They tricked us on all counts, and I state calmly that they tricked us from one day to the next. They made us look fools, and it was difficult for the army to take that, because it -- it made us look very naive, the fact that we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try and make a comparison with what is happening today. It seems that North Korea is trying to launch a rocket, and I think the Security Council will meet. I think they're meeting right now. This is what was happening with you at the time. It was supposed to be implement, and it wasn't implemented. So as far as you know in Geneva did Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen told immediately about this? Were they told immediately about this? You might not know, I don't know. I'm just putting the question to you in case you might have information on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what they were informed of, Your Honour, but I do know that all the proposals that came forward and were accepted by Mate Boban, that is to say the Croatian side, I know that, and that they were signed by Franjo Tudjman, and that we had every hope that it would mark the end of the war. That's what I do know. You but let me give you another example with your permission, concerning Vakuf. You will remember the so-called Cuban crisis when on the territory of a sovereign state, the Russians brought in rockets. Now, the Americans wouldn't -- wouldn't have thought that those rockets were targeting birds and trained on birds; so that's the answer, either take your weapons away or we're going to defend ourselves. And that was the Vakuf situation. Just imagine they're shooting at Americans and killing 5, 10, 15, and you're waiting there calmly taking it all and then when you respond somebody comes in here and says, You attacked first. No. It was a justified, logical, provoked military action which was carried out professionally and completed on the 22nd with the prohibition of touching Gornji Vakuf or the population there or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, first a technical matter. On point 8, would you be so kind as to read that little sentence on page -- on the second page, number 8. "The commanders," is the first word, "zapovjednici."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rajic is addressing in this item to brigadier Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry I just asked you to read please in your language the text, and I will explain why afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 8: "The commanders of units from item 6 of this order shall submit their daily reports to me by 2000 hours at the latest."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those who have followed the English text will have noted that it is miswritten. Instead of number 6, the reference is to paragraph 8. So that is a mistake which must be corrected. And my -- my question with regard to this is: Are you aware of these reports that Bozo Rajic demands to be sent to him daily were ever actually sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, but with a great deal of certainty I can claim that apart from the reports from the HVO, he did not receive any reports from the VRS and from the BH Army, and I can say that with 99.99 percent certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. The second question is I want to point to point 5 where it is -- reference is made "until the final agreement." This gives the impression that there is a provisional element in this order. How would you interpret this reference to "until the final agreement"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, as far as I know, in Geneva an agreement was reached on the cease-fire, but since Mr. Petkovic was up there, he will be in a better position than I am to know what. But here it says: "On the basis of what was agreed in Geneva this is what we've done," and it goes on to say if a final agreement is reached, an agreement that would signify any changes or that any new orders should be signed to operationalise this agreement in Geneva, then this would be amended. This is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in answering the question put to you by my fellow Judge, you said that Halilovic and Mladic never wrote any reports. Now, as far as you know, and I'm sure I will ask him the question when General Petkovic comes to testify, if he does, as far as you know did General Petkovic ever make a report to tell Mr. Bozo Rajic that things were not working in regions 3, 8, and 10; did he do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour, but I do know for a fact because I was with Rajic at the time that he was fully briefed. He was fully aware of the fact that -- the fact that the HVO refused to implement it, that it didn't affect the other two army. Now, whether Petkovic sent him any reports or not, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, if later on but maybe General Petkovic Defence will show us that, if we find a report by General Petkovic sent to Bozo Rajic, according to you would that mean that that would demonstrate the good faith of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably, yes, but I was in the field, and I will be testifying later, and you will see from other documents it was goodwill, but not only goodwill but strong, aggressive will to reach, to achieve peace. That is what existed on the part of the HVO. You will see that from other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you have to demonstrate good faith, not just, you know, with speeches. You need also to act, but we'll see that later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. General Praljak, there's one element in one of the answers that you gave to me which surprises me somewhat, and the same issue has been addressed by the president. You know 99 percent for sure what Mladic and Halilovic did not do, but you simply say you don't know, you have no idea what your immediate military neighbour within the HVO, Mr. Petkovic, that is done. Isn't that a bit surprising? You know what happens on the other side, and you have no idea what happens on your side. I find that a bit surprising, I must say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, no, it's not surprising at all. Until the 22 to 23rd I spent a couple of days in Mostar after that date and I know what happened, and I know for a fact from Bozo Rajic that he definitely did not receive anything from Sefer and from Mladic, and he know that he knew what the HVO was doing. I simply don't know whether Petkovic gave him anything. It's possible that he did, but it's not in any kind of a contradiction, knowledge that something was not done. You receive it from a man. Well, Mladic -- well, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, Mladic was laughing his head off because the war was just getting under way. He found this really funny, and you will see from the documents in an hour, an hour and a half -- in an hour or an hour and a half, you will see what Sefer was thinking. You will not get his thoughts about this but in other things. So you don't really have to -- you know too much about the situation because you're down there all the time, so you don't need to have a piece of paper for everything. I simply know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll continue. Ms. Pinter, one thing that escaped me earlier, you did not submit an IC list today. Is there a reason for this?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For last week? I have information because I saw a person nodding that the IC list for last week was submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will check.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I'm told. Now, to let you know, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, when you asked General Praljak whether Lord Owen and Vance knew about the talks and the events in Vakuf; I would like to bring up document P01240, dated the 21st of January, 1993. It's a discussion in the office of President Dr. Franjo Tudjman dealing with this issue. This transcript has already and admitted. It's an exhibit. It was tendered by Jadranko Prlic Defence as part of their presidential transcript motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, would you look at the document because it follows naturally in what you've been saying in answer to Their Honours. 2D00441. The date is the 21st of January, 1993. It's again signed by Bozo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again he talks about the principles from the peace agreement, because obviously the principles were signed at the time, and he again issues an order of the same form. It's to be extended until the conclusion of the peace talks in Geneva, so let's have peace until peace talks in Geneva are concluded. This is again -- the essence is the same as in the previous document and in everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Or, rather, could you please look at P01343. It's the official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date is the 19th of January, 1993. It's the decision that bears that date, the Official Gazette was issued on the 29th of January, 1993. It's the decision of the president, Alija Izetbegovic, declaring the order of the defence minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina null and void. This document confirms what we've heard from you about how the joint order on the establishment of peace and resubordination, if we can call it that, was stopped. It's already been admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here Mr. Izetbegovic says, "Rajic, you don't have the right to do anything of the sort," although it was agreed that he would issue such an order. But the question remains why Mr. Izetbegovic, because you saw from the transcripts that he agreed to such a thing, why didn't he himself sign it? That's precisely what we've been hearing about here, and that's that Mr. Izetbegovic was playing for a number of reasons that we can now think a double game. That's one thing. And another thing is that this whole issue surrounding this order that was supposed to be the cause of war, on the 19th of January, 1993, it no longer exists. So he invalidated it, declared it null and void, and we were back at square one without any consequences. His generals probably told him or whoever, Silajdzic had already been telling him that in Zagreb as Antun Vrdoljak testifying --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to start objecting, Mr. President, when the witness starts speculating. I've been letting it go, but we're going to start objecting when the witness leads off with a "probably," attributing based on speculation motives behind what other people have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, your objection is on the transcript, but you are not entitled to raise an objection vis-a-vis Defence strategy developed by the witness. Let him develop his theory. During your cross-examination, you can demonstrate that everything he's saying is wrong. So what do we have here? We have an order by the minister of defence which is very precise, which is an implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan alongside with that of the HVO. Mr. Izetbegovic, a few days later, publishes a decision that rescinds the order given by his defence minister by stating that he had not the legal authority to execute this order and this order was anti-constitutional. This raises a whole series of issues. Mr. Praljak, as far as you know, do you remember whether the minister of defence stepped down after this reaction by Mr. Izetbegovic? Was he set aside? Did he have to step down, or did he remain in government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't want to speculate. I don't know the exact answer to that, but I think that he remained in the government. I don't want to speculate, but I can repeat: A, the order that was signed by Mr. Bozo Rajic and the people from the HVO, Prlic, Stojic, Petkovic, was agreed in Zagreb with Mr. Izetbegovic, in the presence of two high-ranking representatives of the international community who acted as mediators in the peace process. B, I took part in that. C, Mr. Izetbegovic on the 19th of January declared this order null and void. So let's leave it at that, that I don't know why that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to say two things. Firstly, on principle I would respectfully disagree that Mr. Praljak the right and the duty as a witness to issue speculations, and I think he, himself, agrees. But the second point is number II of the letter -- or the order of Mr. Izetbegovic we are looking at. If you look at number II, as I read it, but I, of course, read the translation, the reason is he says only the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is competent to sign such an order. So it's not matter of whether Mr. Bozic is still in office, but it's a matter of whether, according to Mr. Izetbegovic, the minister of defence is legitimate to sign such an order or not. Of course I'm -- I will not even attempt to speculate about whether he's right or wrong. I mean, definitely not saying that this is the effective and correct legal argument, but it is what in my view emerges from this letter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we'll get back to this, I'm sure we will, a little later today, because your counsel will certainly have follow-up questions. We are reaching the end of the tape, so we need to have your 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor to the registrar who is going to give us a famous IC list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The second IC list tendered by the Defence of Witness Slobodan Praljak shall be given Exhibit IC1018. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we took our break. You were interrupted. You wish to say something else.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I wish to say is that in this document Mr. Izetbegovic actually says that the minister of defence is not competent to issue that kind of a document. Needless to say, I, myself, don't know whether he had been competent so to do or not. But we heard here in court, and I was familiar with the constitution of the -- constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and without wishing in any way to actually dabble with law too much, I can confirm that neither is Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, according to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina was able to serve a third term of office as president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for that matter. So the Presidency themselves changed the rules on the election of the president of the Presidency in order to enable Mr. Izetbegovic to serve this third mandate -- third term as president, whereas according to the actual rule, he had -- he was under the obligation to relinquish that post and cede it -- hand it over to a Croat. And the Croats didn't carry, in fact, and the Serbs conceded just to peace -- to keep peace in the House. Yes. And the witness is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter could not hear the counsel because of the overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the issue you've just raised had already been mentioned when a witness came to testify, and we had been told that taking it in turns was a rule which prevented Mr. Izetbegovic from holding this mandate. This is something that's been said already, and we know this. Let's proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have to correct the transcript in a section which I think is important. Page 39, lines 1 and 2. General Praljak said that the Serbs didn't actually care about it and that the Croats agreed in order to keep peace in the House, whereas in the transcript it is vice versa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly. The Croats -- the Serbs really didn't care at all about Bosnia and Herzegovina and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic as president of the Presidency. They had their parallel structures of power, and the Croats actually gave in. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now we shall move to document 3D02637. This is Shrader's book, "The Muslim-Croat Civil War in Central Bosnia," and for Their Honours and all others, this book is in binder -- Central Bosnian. General, this is the book that you wished to talk about today. It refers to Central Bosnia, but it is a book which gives an overall overview of events. So please be so kind as to tell their -- to point out to Their Honours the parts which you consider to be of relevance for understanding the situation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here page 25 in the introduction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In English, it's 3D33-0247, and in the Croatian version it is 3D33-0143.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Shrader in this part, Dr. Charles Reginald Shrader, who in 1964 graduated cum laude history, historical sciences at Vanderbilt University, and also completed the American Infantry College of the American army, and the US college for commands and Main Staff members, 7 the NATO university, university college. That was in 1994. And also in Rome the highest military school of the North Atlantic Alliance. So he wrote this book, and I'm going just to take some short excerpts from this book. Here he speaks about Jajce --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would just like a little comment, Mr. Praljak. You have stressed that he made his doctorate cum laude. In what scale is that? What is the best? What is the second, the third, the fourth? I can tell you what the rules are in the universities I know. There are four levels of quality. The lowest is rite then comes cum laude, and then calms magna cum laude, and then summa cum laude. Is this what the scale that was applied here also? If you know, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's Columbia university, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Columbia must be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall quote: "In 1964 he graduated with exceptional distinction (cum laude) historical sciences at Vanderbilt University. At Columbia University he defended in 1976 his doctoral thesis dealing with medieval history," and on as I enumerated earlier in the organisations of the US army, and I cannot tell you any more than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's -- thank you. That's quite all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So here he describes what happened to and with Jajce, and he again refers to 30.000 refugees, which is the number that I also have mentioned myself who fled via the Vietnam Road which I drew for you as the road between the hills. So they fled to Travnik. And he goes on to say -- he says that there were mutual recriminations between the HVO and the ABiH and the BH Army, because of abandoning the defence of the city and that the civilian authorities were confronted with the problem of a formidable number of refugees, which of course is correct, and then he also adds that: "Therein lay the seed of the coming conflict." And as for the subject how the refugees would actually contribute to the conflict which was coming is something that I've already developed and talked about, and Madam Thatcher, Baroness Thatcher also grasped this problem in its entirety, comprehensively. He goes on to say that in respect of the -- that four, the government of Mr. Izetbegovic, the refugees were both a problem and a favourable, favourable development. The favourable development was that a large number of men refugees were simply motivated to exact revenge on both Serbs and the Croats as -- as well. He continues to say that they were not ready for any actions worth mentioning against the Serbs, but that with the arrival of the Mujahedin and due to the large influx -- large influx of able-bodied men in the area, that the army was already by that time able to set up units that were capable of carrying out offensive actions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel please not overlap. The interpreter cannot hear both speakers at the same time. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I repeat: The English version page is 3D33-0248, and the Croatian 3D33-0144.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shrader considers that contrary to the conventional wisdom, the Croat-Muslim conflict was accelerating the fall of Jajce and the influx of refugees that it wasn't the Vance-Owen Plan that was doing that, and he also states that the argument is fallacious that the Croats should be accused for trying prematurely to apply the plan in the provinces, that that had been the source of conflicts; that it was post hoc and proctor hoc thinking that was mistakenly applied and that he can say -- yes, he can say that the conflict actual at this erupted on the 14th of January, 1993, two dates after the cantonal division according to the Vance-Owen Plan had been completed in Geneva, which of course they couldn't have known that quickly really. He also refers to another thesis which was advanced by Franjo Nakic in fact before this court and which myself also will be showing in a document about Mostar, namely that -- I shall not say as Mr. Nakic that had there been no refugees there would not have been any conflicts in the area as well as in Mostar, but it's quite certain that the refugees on their part who had no guarantees whatsoever of ever returning to the territories from which they had been expelled and the majority in fact did not return to Republika Srpska, the vast majority of them never returned, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I apologise, Counsel, for the interruption. I've been looking at the English version of the book, and I may have missed it, but I'm not able to see and it might be helpful if the general could tell us, if he knows, the basis of the information on which Mr. Shrader is making these conclusions or observations that are being tendered to the Trial Chamber, whether he is someone who is in the area at the time, whether he was participating in Vance-Owen negotiations, whether he was in Central Bosnia, or whether this is a historical study based upon documents that he read after the fact. I think it would just be useful to know what his perspective is in terms of having made this book, if the general knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Shrader at that time was not in the area. He had documents at his disposal, and he did spend time, quite some time, in Central Bosnia later on studying not only the documents but also talking to the various people. And then he wrote a book that he signs his name to, just as you, Mr. Prosecutor, wrote the indictment on the document -- based on the documents that you had at your disposal, although you were not in Central Bosnia at that time or on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In his footnotes, he always states what documents he is referring to and what events, and the footnotes have been translated. So I can move on now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, General. The number of the page where the footnote is referring to this latest -- last portion is footnote 5 in the Croatian, but in English it is 3D33-0312, and all the footnotes in the English version are at the end of the book. The whole of the book is in e-court, and the footnotes are on the page I've just quoted, and we have handed over the book to the OTP. I think we did that about a month ago, if not more.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So now we can move on to page 74 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, General. The Croatian page is 3D33-0145, and for the English it is 3D33-0249 to 3D33-0250.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Shrader talks about the three important points that the Western armies have, and that is the so-called three C, command, control, and communications, the three-C system. And he clearly states that there were criminal and extremist elements both in the HVO and in the BH Army, and he focuses in particular on the problem of General Blaskic. Obviously he saw from the documents that in fact it was not possible in Central Bosnia to have a -- to have effective control -- command and control, command and especially not control. As a high-ranking officer who had been to the best military schools, it was obvious that the system of control and command was difficult to implement even when you had highly disciplined armies and well-trained armies and men, and this was particularly impossible when the soldiers and -- and officers were volunteers and when the influence of local political authorities on the selection and dismissal of subordinate commanders was prevalent and when there were independent units that were not responsible to anybody, and when there is general chaos attending this war -- this defensive war, which led to a rise in crime, in common criminality, and when you had very poor communications. And you were able to see that the political representatives of Central Bosnia asked me to return to Central Bosnia. I know that because I was up there, and I know the animal force that you needed to exert in order to fight. And I managed to do that in order to establish some sort of control and law and order and to put a stop to the criminal groups that were rampant and to prevent everything getting out of control. Of course, Blaskic found this much more difficult to achieve than I did because there was a difference between the two of us both in levels of education and strength. Well, in many aspects, many things. Furthermore, he goes on to speak about the newly established units, about people who were friends and came from the same village, and the fact that the command -- that you had to deserve command to be able to command the people and that the people were elected from amongst themselves. And we'll see when we get to the Main Staff at the time when I was the commander of the Main Staff just how much lack of respect there was, lack of respect for any order issued. And then he goes on to say that there were no barracks, which meant that the soldiers went home, taking their weapons with them, and so on and so forth. He speaks about the political influence, and this is to be found on page 76.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on in the book, I have a question for you. The author of this survey, who is an American, so someone who at first-hand is neutral in the face of other warring parties, this is in footnote on the page 51, you are mentioned. The person realise on the Kordic and Blaskic trials. This seems to be the main source of information here. I also noted that he relied on documents from the US Defence Department. So this person has been able to access a great number of documents. Why didn't you ask this person to come as an expert witness for your defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my answer, Judge Antonetti, is simple. Not enough time, and secondly, I thought that the gentleman had already written this book, so that the book signed by him was legitimate and gives us all the credentials we need. So I thought that if we tender the whole book into evidence, then we needn't bring in Mr. Shrader, although we did give it some thought and we were in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd just like to add to what the general has said this: A very prosaic reason: The limited resources that the Defence has to finance an expert witness of such a calibre that this person would no doubt be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was -- the Prosecution was about to make an objection, although it's probably more for later, whenever the book is tendered into evidence, but what's happening here is that the Defence is try to get expert testimony in to evidence. The person appears to have qualifications. He's making observations and reaching conclusions about issues concerning command and control of the HV in Central Bosnia during the time. Now, of course they can tender the book, but what is not going to happen is that the Prosecution's not going to have an opportunity to cross-examine this gentleman. So two things are happening. We have expert information or information that's being tendered as essentially expert testimony and conclusions. At the same time we don't have someone here in the courtroom who will be subject to cross-examination on the conclusions that are being tendered, and it's on that basis and perhaps others that the Prosecution will be objecting to this book or parts of it being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
