utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, what you have said is on the record, but I must say that personally, if I had known about the existence of this book when the expert came, I could have put more relevant questions to the expert in question, because I had no idea that this survey existed. In what way is that expert better than the other one, a former colonel from the US army. So you see you're right when you say what is important is the expert witness. You're quite right when you say that, and that's why I put the question to the Defence, "Why didn't you call this witness?" The Defence answered by saying, "Well, we learnt about this rather late and we don't have enough resources to call this witness." Whatever the case may be, we have a number of documents before us. If the Defence would like to tender these documents, then you can make your observations and the Trial Chamber will rule on this. Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I'd just like to add that this book as the general has already said was written on the basis of documents and refers to specific documents throughout so that documents were presented and will be presented in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may just add one point. It's very similar to hearsay evidence, Your Honours, and so if you have the documents and the documents are presented, then you can use the documents and draw conclusions, and if those conclusions are similar to the ones that are being drawn by the gentleman, there's no reason why weight should not be given to Mr. Shrader's opinions. So I don't think there's anything unusual with what is happening here. For instance, we had used Lord Owen's book. Lord Owen absolutely refuses to come and testify for anybody. He was a prime candidate to -- you know, for us, but he would not come. Nonetheless, he wrote a book based on documents, based on meetings. So you triangulate in this instance. So I don't think -- obviously you can't give the entire weight, but I think there is some merit into considering that there is a limited amount of resources provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, this is something I did not know about. I didn't know that Lord Owen refused to come, because did -- had you intended to call him? You could have subpoenaed him if you wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, subpoenaing somebody and then actually bringing him over are two different things. And secondly, once you drag somebody over here who doesn't wish to be here you've just made him into a hostile witness and obviously makes it much more difficult to get positive information from the gentleman. That's the reality of the practice, and I can assure you over the years I have subpoenaed witnesses, and it's one thing when you're talking to them out of court, but when you force them to come, they're quite different. And this -- Lord Owen, to be quite candid is a very high personality, and obviously he chooses not to testify for any party. So it's not like he's taking sides. Others have agreed to testify it, but even with Holbrooke as you may know, dragging him over here and then negotiating with the American government as to what he will and will not say, you know, how does that -- so we are obviously with certain witnesses we are at, you know, under difficult conditions. I did, in fact -- for the record, I did meet with Mr. Shrader. I flew over to the United States and met with the gentleman. It's quite a difficult task to bring somebody like him here over given the resources that are made available to the Defences and the amount of time. So then one has to decide how best to proceed with their case in light of the fact that we are joined together, have limited resources, and hopefully we're hoping that some will covering certain topics. But getting back to your point, I don't see any reason why the Trial Chamber, which has a much deeper pocket than the Defence, can't call Mr. Shrader if they feel that, you know, they would add to the truth. That could be -- that could be of some assistance. He's in Pennsylvania. He teaches. He used to teach at West Point. So he's quite qualified. He's been to the area. He knows the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What you have said is on the record. Your idea which you have put forward is on the record. Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just to have the correct record -- well, it appears that you confirm -- you observed that the Defence learnt of Dr. Shrader's book too late. That's not true. So I think this might be an interpretation issue. I don't think you said that the Defence learnt about the book too late but that you have just learnt of the existence of the book just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must have misunderstood. I note that you did know about this historian. This is on the transcript now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you said is that we can move on to page 76, which in Croatian is 3D33-0146, and in the English it is 3D33-0252.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to say that most of the matters that Mr. Shrader deals with, the fall of Jajce, the refugees, and so on and so forth, are things that I've already spoken about. So you can ask me about those subjects. Now, in this section Mr. Shrader says something that has been heard several times in this courtroom already, and that is what the political influence in the municipalities was with respect to the appointment of commanders for the units. And he goes on to say that from the United States of America -- that the United States of America had to invest great effort to mitigate the influence that the local political authorities had on the national armies of different states -- or, rather, they're referring to the states of the United States of America. So politicians meddled there, too, in the United States. They meddled in cadres, structure, and so on. And that's on page 77 already.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: For the record and everybody else in the courtroom, the English is 3D33-0251 and 0252. I don't want to interrupt you any more.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he goes on to say that there was an event that we are well aware of, and Mr. Petkovic is well aware of that, and that is that Blaskic needed a month to resolve -- or, rather, to relieve of duty somebody whose name was Tuka, to dismiss Tuka, because the politicians didn't agree to that in the area. And then he goes on -- Mr. Shrader says that in the BH Army, throughout most of the time there was a great clash between Mr. Izetbegovic and the Chief of Staff of the BH Army, Sefer Halilovic, that they were at odds. And I'll be able to show Their Honours that in the days that come. So anyway, there was a clash. They were at odds over such fundamental questions as whether the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ought to defend itself from the Bosnian Serb aggression at all. And then he goes on to say that he does not agree with respect to the people who are passive and possibly traitors too, supports of Izetbegovic, many -- and those backing Sefer Halilovic. So this is something that I've already spoken about, that is to say the fundamental -- fundamentalist Islamic stream which Izetbegovic supported and which together with him or opposed to him made decisions. And Mr. Filipovic addresses that in his own book. So he's an academician, a Muslim, and he says that all this suppressed what little goodwill there was to cooperate among the Bosnian Croats. And then he goes on to say that Izetbegovic and Halilovic quarreled over the police of the Ministry of the Interior and so on and so forth. And I would wrap up with this: The reason why I'm saying this, Mrs. Nika, is because we will be tendering clear documents about that. So now let us move on to page 86.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let me just give the number. 3D33-0148. That's the Croatian. And 3D33-0253 through 3D33-0255. So I don't want to interrupt you, I'm giving the reference now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Shrader here talks about the accusations that the Croatian army is present in Central Bosnia and that this is, of course, the propaganda disseminated by various people from the international community in the field creating a wrong picture of Croatia. And then he also on to speak about the alleged intervention on the part of the Croatian army. And he says that there is no evidence, no proof about the Croatian army presence in Central Bosnia or interfering in any way, which is, of course, more than correct, and we saw this from a document indicating that in late November 1992, the BH Army refused to let through into Central Bosnia what little units there were that were supposed to help Jajce. He goes on to say that the conflict had its peculiarities from one location to another, and that is true. And this is why one should know the history of each town and village, because their histories differ and one can only generalise in one segment of this whole thing. And then he goes on to say that the observers were prone to seeing HV soldiers everywhere, and then he goes on to explain how those claims actually came into being. He says that the HVO was involved in conflict with two enemies. That's page 88. I don't know if you gave us the quote for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The Croatian is 3D33-0149.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then he goes on to say how it happened that this report or this information reached the Secretary-General of the United Nations about the presence of three HV, Croatian army brigades in Central Bosnia. He says that, of course, that this was misinformation provided by UNPROFOR, and of course this propaganda was fomented by the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities. They simply lied. I claim that this is a lie, a lie that was perpetuated because they simply wanted to weaken not only the HVO but Croatia too. In spite of all the evidence about how Croatia treated Bosnia-Herzegovina and the BH Army. Furthermore, he says that nothing of the sort has ever been confirmed, and he quotes Mato Granic. The date is the 11th of June, 1993, where he says that Croatia had no armed formations. And he also quotes me. And in the documents that will be called later about -- well, the documents from the Main Staff from the time when I was active there, I will show quite clearly that this argument is absurd. And he quotes Mr. Bob Stewart at -- at a trial in this very building where he said that generally BritBat did not believe that there was any HV presence in Central Bosnia. And if Mr. Shrader quotes that, then you can find this in the transcript from the Blaskic trial. So famous Bob Stewart, as Shrader says, said that BritBat did not believe there was any HV presence in Central Bosnia. And the UNPROFOR Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-General Sir Roderick Cordy-Simpson also stated that UNPROFOR had no confirmed -- not confirmed such reports and that he personally had never seen any HV troops in the Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Praljak. I wonder whether this is really proper. Here is a gentleman from the United States who assesses the evidence before the Court, practically all of it, and makes conclusion. I don't think this can be called testimony of the witness. I'm sorry, this is really conferring -- conveying to the Chamber someone's considerations which are actually the task of the Chamber. There is a rule that you cannot bring evidence and an expert cannot pronounce himself directly on the finding. It's sort of a shortcut rule. Mr. Karnavas knows what I'm referring to and can give the correct term of it. And Mr. Khan definitely is also -- I'm the only one that is not very, very conversant with this, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, basically they cannot be testifying on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: An expert cannot be testify on the ultimate issue. That is up to the Chamber to make a decision. Perhaps a matter of technique, if for instance the general were to be asked a series of questions about events and perhaps make reference to the book maybe that might be one way of showing how General Praljak's intimate first-hand knowledge is consistent with the conclusions drawn by the gentleman. That may be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That might definitely be more appropriate, because I think this is really a bit -- goes very, very close, at least, to ultimate issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, my fellow Judge is absolutely right to make this observation. Your counsel and you -- this book mentions -- talks about two witnesses, Colonel Bob Stewart and General Cordy-Simpson. Obviously these two gentlemen testified. They were probably Prosecution witnesses. I assume they were. So it's up to your counsel to find their testimony in the Blaskic case and to confront you with it, i.e., say, Mr. Stewart says this, what do you believe of it? General Cordy-Simpson says this, what do you think of it? And your counsel who is very -- knows her job, should also show you part of the judgement in the Blaskic case where the Judges out of the ideas [as interpreted] drew the conclusion that the HV were actually present and then the four Judges on the bench here when they deliberate will draw the necessary inferences from this. So this is the way the evidence must be produced. It's a technical problem. I believe that you must think about this with your counsel, but my fellow Judge was absolutely right. You cannot about it in the way you are proceeding at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence counsel and the Prosecution will deal with that. It seemed to me as we talked this is what I am saying. I claim this. I know that when the accused claims something that his claim is always under suspicion of being untrue. That's only natural, and that's why I tried to find people who are not biassed, people who are impartial, and people who wrote books who have enough education in the field which they covered in their books, and this is why I bring this up to you, Your Honours. This is -- what I've been saying is true, and Mr. Shrader confirms that. This is what I wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, when you are stating something, you're stating something under oath, and this does have a certain probative value, but there is what you're saying under oath and there is what a colonel in the British Army can say. And you know that the colonel in the British Army is more neutral than you are, of course; so what he says will have more probative -- will have more weight anyway than what you will say, so you can state whatever you want but you also have to back everything with other elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a procedural question that has been of concern to us. Mr. Praljak could in his testimony on certain topics simply refer to a book, in this specific example, Mr. Shrader's book or some other book, and say you will find the situation in such and such a book. The problem with the Rules of Procedure in this courtroom which would not make it possible for us to tender this book into evidence. This book is evidence. A book about those topics written by qualified -- by a qualified person. In political sense Margaret Thatcher about political issues. Mr. Filipovic who was an insider. They have probative value, and I'm sure that the Judges would like to see that because this is important. But according to the Rules of Procedure that govern our work here in this courtroom, we cannot tender a single page from a book or a document unless we talk about. And this is why Praljak, after he has already testified about most of these topics, he now says, he now demonstrates that a qualified person shares his opinions and views, and I have to say, perhaps, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the only difficulty that my fellow Judge justly rose is that your client has been reading a page from a book. That's fine, but he could have answered Mrs. Pinter's question in the following way: He could have said, I always stated that the Croatian army was not present in Central Bosnia, and the best proof of this is what is written in this book; and he could stop there and then either you or your fellow counsel could say, Well, in this book we have mention of Bob Stewart, and he's quoted; and then you could present to your client what Stewart said in the Blaskic case. That's the way to proceed. In order to receive a -- to receive anything, the Chamber must check relevance and probative value, possible probative value. This is what we have to take into account to present to -- to admit a document that was shown to a witness. But if the document was not shown to the witness, then the guidelines have to apply but it's more complicated because we have to explain why the document was not presented to a witness, what are the paragraphs involved and so on and so forth. This is here a perfect occasion to show Bob Stewart's and Cordy-Simpson's testimony to Mr. Praljak. Telling them on the transcript, on such and such page, this is what this person said. Do you agree with him, yes or no. And then you can ask for -- we can tender the transcript, transcript which the witness will have either admitted, confirmed or not confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We fully agree with your approach, but again we have this technical problem. As we were preparing for the scope of the testimony of General Praljak and primarily bearing in mind the time that we have at our disposal because we can't get out of that framework, we decided that we would achieve more, that we would be more efficient, we would let General Praljak say more if he were allowed to go through those parts that he thinks support his arguments without our interference. Of course my colleague could ask 120 questions and lead him through all the pages of this book, but I don't think that I have to tell you that this will take much more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one detail. In footnote 42 at page 3D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. The counsel is kindly asked to speak more slowly when quoting numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Shrader, the author of this book -- let me repeat the number 3D33-0316. In footnote 42 provides clear reference for Bob Stewart's testimony and the testimony by Sir Roderick Cordy-Simpson. That was on the 4th of August, 1999. And in the book itself these are direct quotes, which means -- the quotation marks indicate that these are quotes, but if, Your Honours, you want us to put to the general the testimony from those witnesses from the Blaskic case we will do so if we have enough time. It's just -- it's all a matter of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm concerned about how far this is going off track. Books play a role in this trial. I think those of us from different backgrounds have come to accept that. Books by Margaret Thatcher or Lord Owen or Mr. Alagic are books written by people who were there personally participating in events and writing a book about it afterwards; and the Trial Chamber under the procedural rules that it has laid out agrees to accept books or parts of the books, accepting, of course, that anyone who writes a book might be writing it in a way that puts themselves in better light or for whatever motives they may have to recount a story or history in a particular way, but the Trial Chamber knows that, and the Trial Chamber, I assume, takes that into account when it considers the weight to assign excerpts of books. Now, this book is different. This book is not written by someone like Lord Owen or Margaret Thatcher who was there participating in the meetings, who was there like Colonel Stewart. This is a person who is an historian who read a lot of documents and may have gone to the area after the fact and talked to these people, and he's made what reads like an expert report. Now, again, we've had historians testify in this case and in this Tribunal, but they come testify, and their reports, their findings and conclusions are subject to cross-examination and questions from the Judges. That's not happening here. So in that respect, this is a different type of written material than just a book written by someone like Margaret Thatcher. The second point, and again this is just for the record, Mr. President, you indicated a willingness or the possibility of accepting transcripts of witnesses who have testified in other proceedings at this Tribunal like Colonel Stewart or Mr. Cordy-Simpson. They were witnesses in the Blaskic case. Colonel Stewart, actually, was a court witness. He was called by Judge Jorda and the Trial Chamber at the end of the Prosecution, Defence case in the Blaskic trial. But, of course, under the rules we have rules that provide for a mechanism of transcripts from other cases to be put into evidence here, and that's called Rule 92 bis or 92 ter, and if the Trial Chamber or if the Praljak Defence wants to tender transcripts of Colonel Stewart or anyone on these issues, certainly they're free to tender that evidence; but to do so again under those rules and satisfying the procedural requirements of those rules as opposed to just sort of throwing them in together with a book that's written by an expert or a -- someone who appears to certainly possess specialised qualifications whose book is being tendered, parts of it being tendered, and not subject to cross-examination. So now we're at a second level where not only can the Prosecution not cross-examine the gentleman Shrader, but nor are we able to cross-examine Shrader about the transcripts that he's referring to and parts that he may or may not have relied upon. So we're really getting into a deeper level of remoteness and fairness in terms of the Prosecution's ability to deal with this evidence, because it's becoming increasingly separated from the ways that we tender such evidence of experts and other witnesses here in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Prandler has something to say, just a minute, but before my fellow Judge takes the floor, I have something to add. I share Mr. Stringer's point of view. The Defence could have asked this Shrader to write a 92 ter statement, after which -- you know, at the end of which he could have said, you know, I'm an historian, I work for the US army, or whatnot. This is my educational background and career elsewhere. I'm interested for -- in Yugoslavia for such and such reason. I'm very neutral. This is the result of my work. You could have added this on your witness list. And as Mr. Stringer just said, the Prosecution could have asked for this person to be cross-examined. And you would have tendered the statement. It wasn't wasting any of your time because you're not putting any questions, and then we would have allotted two or three hours to Mr. Stringer for cross-examination. This would have been a technical procedure to admit this, but I believe that Judge Prandler has something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do not want to take your time, but I would like to add my voice to the concerns raised by my fellow Judges here and the concern of -- of the caution. Mainly, I would take the other point which probably has not been yet so discussed and consultated upon, and it is the question that this book is in a way concentrating on, and I quote the title, "Civil War in Central Bosnia." Now, it is in Central Bosnia, which of course I am ready to consider to look into and to study, but no doubt a major part of this book and what we are reading here, and I try to look at it in the meantime when we have this discussion here, they are mainly on those issues which are not within the indictment. And I think that it should also be borne in mind that although again I say that I am not against any kind of witness statement or also expert studies, but on the other hand, we should really concentrate on what we have at our hands, i.e., the issue of the indictment. So I would like to hear some explanation about this also from Mr. Praljak and from the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I should just like to caution -- in fact, I should respond to your comment that this book refers to Central Bosnia and that is not the subject of the indictment. And in that connection I should like to draw attention to paragraphs 33, 34, the joint criminal enterprise, and the assertion in the indictment that Croatian forces, the forces of the Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina, in other words, were the ones who started the conflict in all areas, in -- of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I should like to draw your attention to your decision on the acceptance of established facts and in connection with which we were given the right to present evidence to the contrary. I should only like to add that the onus probandi is on the Prosecution and not the Defence. With this book as well as with some other books, the Defence only wished to demonstrate that there also exist other possibilities, and General Praljak, from the very beginning of his defence -- or of his statement, rather, from the 4th of May up to this date has stressed and underlined time and again and also presented documents which show the presence or nonpresence of Croatian forces in the areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e., the areas of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. In other words, General Praljak has so far in countless situations spoken about the circumstances which are quoted here and which actually confirm his statement, his allegations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I believe we should not go on with this book. There is nothing that is too interesting. I wanted to show the view presented there about the presence of the Croatian army in the -- in the area of Central Bosnia and what the possibilities were of controlling the HVO in -- in conjunction with the problems of the organisation of the army, control, communications -- control and communications, and the involvement of political echelons. Needless to say, I wanted to show how this attack of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which Alagic and others testify about in their books also spilled over to the south and how this chaos developed. The gist -- the gist of the problem is who manages the chaos, who generated the chaos. What were the possibilities of controlling it, and why am I guilty or what am I guilty of? That is the essence of this case, the general comprehension of the situation to see whether these six people did have the power, if they did have the will and how much power they did have to stop all that. This is what I'm saying and other people are also saying. I'm saying what power I had, what the extent of my power was and how I used it. Because the crux of it, where there is some phenomena which took place will be ascribed to the people who were down there. That is the essence of the thing. For instance, to me, was my power such that this war situation could evolve without any war crimes being committed and how much I'm to blame in that context. That is the sense. Because in every war you can say that a soldier has done this or that and then just lock up a general or some other superior. That's why I assert that the overall policy of France, America, the Serbs, Alija, the fundamentalists, actually engendered something that I do not want to be responsible for. Just because I remained there amid that chaos rather than go to Germany. And I could go to Germany because I was of the proper age. That's it. So we've just extracted passage. You try and seek to prove something and you can prove anything. Let us not discuss this book any more. Thank you very much. Because I believe to go on would just mean that we would only develop something else, and what I can't claim is what Mr. Shrader confirms, that the attack of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Central Bosnia had been planned and that it amounted to aggression and that they barely managed to hold out until the end. This is what Alagic and Shrader and Praljak claim. That's it from me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to make one comment for the record with respect to Judge Prandler's observations. I've read the book. In fact, I've read it several times, and I can -- I can attest that based on what is being presented in the indictment, it is highly relevant what Mr. Shrader does. Now -- because he provides alternative plausible explanations to events that are directly linked to the indictment and links to the joint criminal enterprise. That's why you can't just dissect something and say this is Central Bosnia, therefore, it's not relevant, because if I may recall everyone's attention to the fact that the Prosecution has argued extensively that there was reverse ethnic cleansing in Central Bosnia. But I understand the general's frustration. Perhaps we can get back to this book. But I just want to make sure on the record what is in that book is directly related to the -- to the joint criminal enterprise, who started what, because there's a trickle-down effect, sort of a domino effect, and you just can't separate it and say well, that's Central Bosnia. It is highly relevant to this -- to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I thank Mr. Karnavas for his explanation. Let me also for the record to say the following: That I have never doubted that certain parts of the book, and I tried to look at those parts during our discussion here, they are relevant. I do not deny that. I said that the book as a whole and -- and it is about Central Bosnia and apart from certain parts, which I admit they have certain bearing on the issue -- on the issues before us on the indictment. Nevertheless, the bulk of the book is not what I -- what I see from this one which would be relevant for us. But again I said I am pleased to read it as a -- I will read it as a whole during our next couple of days. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, to round up on the subject, you said a while ago, "I claim that the ABiH had planned these attacks in Central Bosnia." Fine, you've said it, and you are under oath, but now technically speaking, your counsel should have put the question to you this way: A book has been written by a well-known American, and so on, and you say yes this book exist. And then she puts a question to you and says why do you wish to talk about this book, and then you can answer by saying, Well, I claim that it was the ABiH that launched its attack throughout 1993 in Central Bosnia. And then she says, what do you rely on to say this? And then you say, Well, all you need to do is look at Annex B of the book where all the documents of the 3rd Corps are proof of this. So your counsel then says, I shall show you the document pertaining to the 7th Brigade, and so on and so forth. This is how you should proceed. I'm not going to give you a lecture on how you are to present your evidence or adduce it in the most efficient manner. Mrs. Pinter, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, counsel are not that much militarily educated, but here on page 119 you can ask me a question as recommended to you by His Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just turn this page. So on page 119 -- pages 119 and 120, in particular page 120 of the book, which in the English language version is 3D33-0264 and in Croatian 3D33-0161 there is reference about trial attacks of the army -- of the ABiH army in January 1993. We have already discussed about the situation in Gornji Vakuf, and not only Gornji Vakuf, we spoke about Travnik. Travnik is in Central Bosnia and there were problems there as well. The events in Central Bosnia and the events in Mostar, i.e., in the Main Staff which is in Mostar and the events in Novi Travnik and Gornji Vakuf, Zenica, and Busovaca are also events also described by Mr. Shrader in his book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim and that is what I have been saying here and it is also attested to by Mr. Shrader that the trial attacks by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina started in January 1993, that already in 1992, towards the end of 1992, a number of brigades of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina deployed at key points in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, well, it's fine for you to say that, but then your counsel should show you a document that states that the brigades were deployed in the Lasva Valley. Then she shows you the document, and then you explain that this document proves that they had prepared the ground beforehand and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, believe me, I have many people on my team, so a hundred people couldn't be able to cover each unit. So Mr. Shrader states here very precisely and gives a map of the deployment of the forces of the 3rd Corps; and he says, this is KCD 189, and he shows the disposition of the 351, 309th, and parts of the 7th Muslim Brigade. And from this disposition it is evident that they are directed at the HVO. But this is what Mr. -- or the general in the book also says. The general says this very precisely, he is the commander, and he says, "We have deployed our units behind the back of the HVO and they failed to notice that." This person --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Alagic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This other one. Yes, Alagic. There are so many maps. There is ample evidence. So if Alagic writes that in his book and then Shrader again claims the same thing. And take me, I'm saying the same thing under oath. Then I claim that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that you have clear evidence. You know that the Judges, when they are to determine the question, need to have compelling evidence. They're not going to rely on what you're saying even what you're saying is under oath. This needs to be supported by documents that go unchallenged. For instance, like the deployment of units and a number of reports. This then gives all of this probative value. You know that the Prosecution has another theory, and the theory of the Prosecution is that you had started the attack and launched the attack, and the Prosecution is certainly going to come up with documents that testify to the fact that you were the one that launched the attack. Have you understood what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have understood. But let him show a single document proving that we attacked first. Have we ever seen a document about an attack in Gornji Vakuf, except for the fact that the English officer tells me, Yes on the map that I drew. Well, I drew the map, Your Honours, and I asked the man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you show us documents in support of your theory and if the Prosecution is unable to demonstrate the contrary, then the Trial Chamber will conclude that you are right, but the Trial Chamber cannot reach this conclusion on the sole basis of what this American historian has said. The Trial Chamber needs further evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, I'm fully conscious of that. However -- well, we've been here for three years, and during that space of time I've seen not a shred of evidence about an HVO attack except tactic movements against the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have not seen a shred of evidence showing that we displaced the population in any way from Central Bosnia to fill up Herzegovina that was full of Croats already with yet more Croats. But I don't know what I'm supposed to defend myself against. I claim that the trial attack -- or, rather, the taking of Vakuf happened as I've explained it, and that's what Mr. Shrader said, too, that they wanted to effect control along this Diamond route and that that's how they behaved. And every soldier will make the same conclusion. You can bring anybody in, anybody you like, and they will deduce the same. And I've explained how many times we tried to resolve the problem and all the rest of it. So regardless of what happens next, I have finished with the book. There's no need to go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just by way of information, we've just started discussing Central Bosnia. We haven't even reached the documents. We started with the book, and I think this is the right time for the break.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wanted to make one observation, Your Honour, based on Mr. President's remarks, because it seems to me maybe it was misinterpreted, but it seems as if there's a shifting of the burden of proof. The Prosecution has made allegations they obviously have to prove. Whether the Defence proves or disproves it is another thing, but we don't have -- as the Defence have to convince the Trial Chamber otherwise. They have to convince you. And perhaps it was just a misinterpretation, though I think we're on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I couldn't fail to disagree with you less. I do agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This was certainly not at all in question. The Chamber is very well aware of the fact that it is for the Prosecution to prove the facts it alleges, not for the Defence to disprove but for the Defence, as the case may be, to cast sufficient doubts on the -- on what -- the accusation put forward that we can see that we are not convinced beyond reasonable doubt. That's all the Defence is expected to do, and please do not doubt that this is firmly in the mind of each and every Judge on this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, before the break --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Trechsel. Look at the problem with the Croatian army. All we have from the Prosecutor is that some people saw some things. One of them saw a division wherein he saw 50 people at Metkovic. We have to look at my orders that the HVO must not go there, then Susak's, then Stipetic's, then draw the maps. Your Honour, it's like this: I am simply don't know how many arguments to the contrary are sufficient for me to be even partially certain I have explained what is meant by the Croatian army, because that's how this trial is going. I always have this fear, well, in quotation marks, that I am invoking Shrader to help me out and Bob Stewart to help me out, to say it again and again and yet again; and wasn't it up to the Prosecutor to say here you have the piece of paper - and they've got all the papers down there - from the Main Staff of the HV where five brigades have been sent to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Had he shown that, I would have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we do not disagree with you. The only issue we have is the Trial Chamber filed judicial notice on the international -- international conflict which is -- has been mentioned in the Blaskic judgement. So there was an international conflict and the Croatian army was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's it. But if you would like to attack this theory, then you have to provide further evidence. We are not reversing the burden of proof. The international conflict has been acknowledged. If you want to make a dent into this, you have to introduce your own evidence. It's for you to counter-attack this theory, otherwise, the Prosecutor doesn't have to do much, because all of this has been said. If you want the Prosecution to cross-examine you, you need to challenge this which has been stated in the Blaskic trial. This is what we would like you to understand. We're going to have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court is back in session. We have one hour left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we're moving on to another area now. What do you know about the referendum of the 19th of July, 1993, held in Knin, according to which the governments of Republika Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska were supposed to meet?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The referendum wasn't held in Knin, it was in the whole area of the two Serbian states as they called them. This one here, the Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was one state. And the other state was the Republika Srpska Krajina in Croatia, in the areas depicted on the map. And already on the 31st of October, 1992, the Prijedor declaration was passed by the Serbs in which they presented the following: That the legal systems in the Republika Srpska Krajina, which is in Croatia, of course, on occupied territory, and Republika Srpska would be identical. The legal systems, I mean. That is to say they would have the same coat of arms, the same flag, the same hymn and everything else that is needed for a joint state. Furthermore, on the 27th of June, 1993, a referendum was held for the Serbs in the Republika Srpska and in -- well, I won't say so-called, but anyway, so-called Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska, the one in Croatia and the one in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the question asked at the referendum was, and I quote -- the question put was: "Are you in favour of independence for the Republika Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska?" And later on with other Serb areas. Unity, unification with other Serb lands is I think what is missing here. Anyway, 98 percent of the population came out for the referendum, 98 percent of the voters. Before that, generals -- the generals of the Army of Republika Srpska and of the Srpska Republika signed an agreement on military assistance in case of attacks, an attack on any portion of Western Serbia, because according to that policy - and we've said that hundreds of times - it was considered that this whole area here in the Republic or Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled by the Serbs were and constituted Western Serbia. Furthermore, on the 30th of May, 1993, at a meeting of the political leadership of the Republic of Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska, Biljana Plavsic put forward a proposal that conclusions be voiced at the assemblies about the formation of a joint Assembly and state of these two sections or two states that I've mentioned before, Republika Srpska Krajina, and the other one was Republika Srpska. And she goes on to say that there was no sense in beating about the bush any more, and Radovan Karadzic said at the time, and I quote: "The aspirations of the people for unification are evident and we must respect them. Those aspirations will be realised either now or later, and a state united in that way will join up with the one east of the Drina River." Republika Srpska, Republika Srpska Krajina would join up with the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What would that mean for the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I keep stressing that when we come to this thesis about an alleged international conflict that is permeating all these discussions -- well, I don't know how to show you this. The Serbs did not attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia separately, but they attacked the Muslims and Croats on the territory of the Republic of Croatia and on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what happened. And had it had had the strength and power to do so as far as I was able to see and reading what international law says, Croatia with its units could have -- well, this state that was taking away a third of its territory could have attacked it at any point anywhere. Croatia did do that in 1995 in Operation Storm, of course when it was given the green light from the international community because they were unable to solve the problem. So the law is the law, and what America says is far more the law than what international law stipulates. That is what I claim.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, in the Republic of Croatia did they endeavour through legal means to resolve or regulate this aspiration with respect to the unification of those two parts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the Sabor, the Assembly took a decision saying that that was invalid. The Constitutional Court -- well, a war isn't solved with the Constitutional Court's decisions but the victory of an army in the field. Unfortunately, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, what we have just been talking about was written in Slavko Degoricija's book. It is not in vain, and that is 3D02656. You've read the book?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, it's hard to follow you. You're saying many things, and sometimes it's a bit difficult to understand you. We have not been seized of Operation Storm. I believe that we agree on this. But you're saying when there was Operation Storm, the international community gave its green light. Can you back this with evidence or is this just speculation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, this is not speculation. There is clear evidence of that, because all the participants thereof clearly stated that once all the plans have fallen through, plans to resolve that situation, then Franjo Tudjman, with the Croatian army, prepared, of course, the liberation of those territories, and according to what I've been saying all this time and we will see later, this thing, well, he -- he tried to bring it into line with, at that moment, the Americans, and literally, literally, when presenting the fact that this had to be done, had the Americans not -- well, the Americans did not explicitly say yes, but with their silence they implicitly say, "Yes, please go ahead. Do it." Holbrooke says that in his book. Various other participants say the same thing. I could give you several sources. He even called us, Holbrooke, saying, well, we can't -- we couldn't solve that, and then we left it to the dogs of war. So he called us dogs of war, Mr. Holbrooke did. Then I go on to say, because I know that, that we were assisted in the way that some top US generals, retired US generals, had come. We paid them that they placed at our disposal drones, pilotless aircraft, so that we could see what was going on in the occupied territory, and the beginning of that operation was seen by Mr. Clinton on his TV set, probably in the Oval Office, and again I say there are all those statements in the books by witnesses who were participants in those events. And this was because they couldn't and didn't want to protect Srebrenica and so on; and astonished by what had happened in Srebrenica and immediately after that the same scenario was being prepared from Bihac, they told the Croatian army, of course to the HVO and the BH Army; but the course of the Croatian army carried out the main assault in order to prevent further massacres of Muslims, primarily, and also of Croats. And this is how the Croatian army reached all the way up to Banja Luka, almost reached Banja Luka. The Serb forces were defeated, but -- and I know that first-hand then, and Mr. Galbraith writes about that even today, and Mr. Holbrooke, asking themselves whether they did the right thing at the time. At the time, under the threat of sanctions, they told the Croatian army to stop, because, Your Honours, before that Milosevic managed to arrange with the international community that he would get 49 percent of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was not under discussion in Dayton. Croats and Muslims came to Dayton, and they were told 51 percent and Serbs got 49 percent. These are the facts, and this is the truth that I can document any which way you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I asked you about the book, "It was not in vain," authored by Slavko Degoricija. Did you speak about the unification of Republika Srpska and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have given a number of it. I think it was 3D02656, and would you be so kind as to assist us by telling us, for instance, in which of some 20 binders we have now surrounding us we have a chance of finding it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the way it looks like. You have it as a separate binder. It's a separate -- it's a separate -- well, it couldn't fight in this binder and it had to be put together as a separate file. And the page that -- the pages that contain -- that deal with the topics that the general has been speaking about are on pages 3D33-12 -- 2167. The English version is 3D41-0420, 3D41-0421, and 3D41-0422.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you said that the referendum was held in the whole of that territory.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What were the results in the end? Did they unite, form a union, or if not, how was this prevented?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the referendum they were unified, but this was prevented by military action. How else? You could not prevent it by decision of the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to add, Your Honours, that when the Croatian generals came and two of them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, US generals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- came and two of them were members of the joint chiefs of staff retired, I personally participated in the formation of this body where they were in because I was at that time a military advisor to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm -- may I? May I? Mr. Praljak, who is the author of this book? Slavko Degoricija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Your Honour, he was -- he was a key man of Franjo Tudjman. He was a high-ranking person in the structure of the Croatian state. Well, I'm not sure now whether he was in the government. I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: He was a deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was a deputy minister. He was the chief negotiator. I know for a fact because I know him personally, and he says in his book at least 150 times, on the orders of President Tudjman, he went to talk with the Serbs, the rebel Serbs, in the Republic of Croatia. And in this respect, some Serbs from this area around Pozega, the central part, Western Slavonia that was also occupied. He was quite successful, and those people modified their extremist political positions, and after the war, they became members of the Croatian parliament representing the Serb people. It's the same, the very same man who for almost a month on the orders of President Tudjman stayed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina trying to convince the people and the leadership to vote in the referendum whereby Bosnia and Herzegovina was able to be recognised as a state pursuant to the Badinter Commission. His name is Slavko Degoricija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, 2009, he was mentioned. That's at page 40008, line 4, and on the 19th of May of this year, at page 40353, line 16. General, now we will move on to a file that's call "General Praljak calms the tensions." It's not in a binder. It's in this form. This is what it looks like. General, could you please go to page 3 -- or, rather, document 3D00542. Before that, I would like to ask you this -- well, we've mentioned Jasmin Jaganjac. He is a man who -- whom you know personally.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about Jasmin Jaganjac?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to repeat myself. I've said that a couple of times already. Mr. Jasmin Jaganjac, we said what he did in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when this document was drafted, he was the military advisor to the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You are familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we get -- I'm not sure that I -- could we get the exhibit number for the document that the general is talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's probably not in the record. That's 3D00542.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You had talks with Mr. Jaganjac.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met with Mr. Jaganjac in Central Bosnia. Well, you've seen the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, but I have not yet been able to locate this document in the immense -- they all look like -- we've got, I don't know, half a dozen of documents that look like that. What is the title exact -- the exact title, because they all have the name of Praljak on the title, which is normal. Is it the one that says annex General settles down?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: No, General Praljak settles down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Oh, you're not even agreed amongst yourselves which one is it? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: "General Praljak settles down the tensions between ABH -- B and H and HVO," November 1992, March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry if I'm a bit -- there's no evil spirit behind it. Please believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, before we move on to this document, I would like you to look at the document. It says the 12th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it doesn't say the 12th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, that's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it says the 12th of February, 1993, because 1992 wouldn't mean anything. There were no weapons in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was no war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You can see that this is number 3. If you look a bit more closely, and it is immensely clear from the document that this document pertains to 1993. So in item number 1 Mr. Jaganjac writes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter, where does this document come from? It's a handwritten document? How did you obtain it? Did you get it from the archives of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? How did it ever land into your hands?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received it from the author.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I think -- well, Your Honours, you know, the Prosecution interviewed Mr. Jaganjac.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, that's not there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Mr. Jaganjac listed the documents that he provided to the Prosecution. I don't know whether he also submitted this document. I'm not sure, but I think that this document is among those documents -- among the documents that Mr. Jaganjac provided to the Prosecution from his personal archive. Unfortunately, the Prosecution has not called Mr. Jaganjac as its witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, we'll check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter, I'm putting this question to you because I'm trying to verify the authenticity of this document. If on 6.45, 1845 hours, on February 12, 1993, Mr. Jaganjac is sending this letter to Mr. Izetbegovic. First, we have no idea how he sends it, with a helicopter, with a bird, or I don't know, the original must have been received by the president of -- Mr. Izetbegovic, President of the Presidency. But if Mr. Jaganjac told you that he gave you this document, it means that when he was writing documents, at the time writing letters, he would be systematically keeping a copy of all these letters? How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well I don't want to commit myself at this point and tell you something for a fact. I'll check that. As far as I know, we did receive some documents from the Prosecution related to Mr. Jaganjac's statement, and through our own fieldwork we managed to obtain some documents. At this point it would be less than serious on my part if I were to tell you specifically what it was. I will give you the correct answer tomorrow morning. I can only tell you that number 3D --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go into private session for a moment, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in item 1 he says that he agreed with me and General Cermak that some materiel should leave for Pazaric, which in Eastern Bosnia [Realtime transcript read in error "Posavina."] I should like to remark here once again, if someone from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in this case Jaganjac, asked for some means, resources, they would usually agree that it should go to Foca, to Pazaric, to Tuzla and so on. But, Your Honours, once that passed through the last check-point of the HVO, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina could take it wherever they wished. We did not follow that convoy any longer as security up to Pazarici or Foca. The moment it left, for instance, the Rama check-point or at another point, the army could transport it wherever they wished, as they wanted. It is important to say here that these two trucks, trailer trucks, each of which carries between 20 and 25 tons, are called by Mr. Jaganjac quite logically a symbolic quantity. Your Honours, it is obvious from this that Croatia sent quantities that Jaganjac called symbolic, these two trailer trucks namely. Then he goes on to say that other quantities will follow as soon as this first quantity is confirmed to have arrived. Then he refers to a statement by Mr. Izetbegovic which has not been studied sufficiently. And then he asked -- he asked me whether we, Boban, and the others had renounced Herceg-Bosna, and I replied, and my response was in accordance with the policy, the then-ruling policy of the Herceg community of Herceg-Bosna that it no longer existed as such because this was, according to the Vance-Owen Plan, that we needed a transitional period. So, Your Honours, what you saw Jadranko Prlic and others do here, namely when they talked about all the effort that needed to be invested in order to structure and organise the new authorities. So it is obvious that the HZ HB was a provisional organisation serving to defend a specific area in Bosnia and Herzegovina because we were better prepared. We had prepared ourselves better for that war. That was it and nothing more. It goes on to say that Boban was being waited for to come from Germany and that pressure would be brought to bear on him to sign this. And Mr. Boban did, indeed, sign it. An entire series of these documents were shown by Mr. Prlic's Defence. And then there only remains the minor problem to the effect that with the -- with the flags of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina there should also be hoisted the flags of the provinces, including, needless to say, and of course, also the flag of the Croatian nation just as you have put it yourself, Your Honour. So the entire problem on the Croatian side was to put up its flags and say thereby yes, we do exist here in this republic, in this state and as part of its flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I -- excuse me. It's just a technical problem. Perhaps it's not that important, but in this number 2, the second sentence here reads: "They find it quite approximate," and this strikes me as a bit surprising. Is the translation correct? I would expect something like "appropriate" rather than "approximate," even more so in that in the next sentence, they say, "There is insufficient investigation." Is it really approximate? I'm looking at Ms. Tomanovic who usually is our linguistic expert in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, you are quite right. I only endeavour to correct the transcript when it is important, and I will do so now, because page 84, line -- just a minute -- 17, there are some words missing. A word is missing. It is "in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Actually, General Praljak said the Croats with their flag wanted to state here we exist here in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly. In the provinces -- in the provinces that have been designate -- had been designated as Croatian, which wasn't quite correct because they were joint provinces, but the Croats had a majority of the population. In those provinces there will be hoisted the flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It will be flown. But in addition to it, we also want a flag to be put up which that province will have as its own specific one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Excuse me general. Let us not go too far. If I may intervene at this point. Page 83, line 2, you said that Pazarici was referred to in this document that it is in Eastern Bosnia. Page 83, line 2. It says eastern Posavina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say for the benefit of Their Honours that Pazarici is a place near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am aware of that. Pazarici is right next to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just reply to His Honour's question, to Judge Trechsel that the translation of the document in question is correct. It is exactly as you read it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, it was probably on the same day when this proposed statement of Mr. Izetbegovic came that he came to talk to me. And apart from that, Susak and I just read it in haste. There was some minor points that needed to be dealt with, but in the long -- but, actually, we were waiting for Mr. Boban to come back. And as I said, the pressure was to be brought to bear on him, but he was the one to make the final decision. I claim, however, that this was also the policy which was followed by Mr. Boban, and it is written on all these documents "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," until peace is established in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So HZ HB was provisional organisation serving for defence purposes. There was no talk of it becoming any kind of a state let alone its annexation to Croatia. And let's go on. Number 3 as regards the flag, that is all clear. And it says here if there is anything controversial, he would inform Mr. Izetbegovic the next day, but we disputed nothing. At least our side did not find anything to challenge. I told Mr. Jaganjac from what I knew and what I had been saying all along, that the situation in Central Bosnia was tense and that according to the information that we all had at our disposal, and I will not show all these documents, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was preparing to attack the HVO. And I asked Mr. Izetbegovic for me to go to Herzegovina and for him to give me two Muslims, two eminent politicians who worked together with me, to Central Bosnia and work to further ease the tensions there. And I say that I will be in Mostar and that our liaison will be Zijad or Safet. Safet Orucevic was the chief figure in the east part of Mostar; and Zijad was, at that time, already, I believe, the president of the SDA for Herzegovina, Zijo Demirovic namely. Now, in item 4, items 4, 5 and on, he reports to Mr. Izetbegovic on things that I had been repeating myself, namely that there is one policy being followed by Adil Zulfikarpasic who was a very rich man as I said before. And he was a Swiss citizen. He had the Bosniak institute. I'm not sure whether it was in Geneva or where. And it goes on to say that Mr. Adil Zulfikarpasic was establishing contacts outside the command structure with Sefer Halilovic and that he actually didn't know its -- it refers to the statements of leading figures that were against the Vance-Owen Plan, in particular that of Sefer Halilovic who considered himself to be man number one in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you will see the words he uses to describe Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Apologise for the interruption. I think unless I'm missing something in e-court we don't have the complete translation in e-court. There's a one-page translation in e-court that only contains points 1, 2, and 3. It does not contain any subsequent points 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation is at 3D28-0801. That's as far as the pages are concerned. The number is 3D00-542 ET.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Actually, counsel's right. There are three documents in e-court and the translation that counsel has just referred me to is indicated in e-court as being an original, meaning the original language document. So that's not correct. So maybe that could be fixed in e-court to indicate that 3D28-0800 is a translation and not the original document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can I conclude? I talked to about all these matters because in a certain way I was -- we already had friendly relations, Mr. Jaganjac and me, that is, after a lengthy period of joint efforts so that our relations evolved to such a point, and I knew that Zulfikarpasic had at a certain point started to influence some of the personnel of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, some of the generals that he actually wouldn't subscribe to an agreement about joint life between the Muslims and Croats and in this -- these parts, and that is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Please look at document 3D03510. This was a military booklet that you have already seen, that you ever held in your hands. Perhaps you have it today. Can you tell Their Honours under what circumstances and how you got it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Pinter, I've talked about it already, when I received it. We cannot repeat things to such an extent. We do not have the time. The booklet is here, but the signature of Mr. Pasalic has faded, but if Their Honours would like to take a look at it, it is already inscribed in the paper. And as you are already familiar with his original signature you will see that it is indeed it. In this way, I also became a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, yet another military formation, if you would like to see it I have a magnifying glass which could be of assistance if you do wish to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, please could you go and fetch the map so that we can have a look at it. I would like the Judges to have a look at it, and we'll also show it to Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, card, not map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While we're looking at it, Mr. Praljak, this is a little bit surprising, and one wonders how come you get something like that. Was it a gesture of camaraderie, of goodwill, something with a more a social than a strictly legal character?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were not, you know, distributing social assistance and benefits in order to give me a document of this kind. If you just remember how many Muslims there had been in the HVO, and of course there were Muslims in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this was given at a time when -- when we thought that we were one army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was using the term "social" in a quite different way, in terms of socialising and having civilised relations, and I -- was there any -- any formal procedure, administrative procedure to get you this or was it just brought as a friendly gesture, symbolic but -- but not really administrative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, if you recall Mr. Arif Pasalic, who was already by now the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had been for a long time in the HVO, a very long time, initially we never looked to see who was what, but we had nothing against the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were one people. We only had to pursue joint objectives, but there were no common political objectives to pursue. Therefore, what evolved developed, this that we have been discussing here and will be discussing for at least a year in this court, another year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if he's not done so already, and I don't think he's done so today, maybe he did the other day when he spoke about this, could the general indicate precisely or as best as he can when he got this and where he was when he received it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can tell you that roughly. When we went -- or, rather, before we set out, Mr. Arif Pasalic and I towards Prozor to calm the situation down there, that's when he, according to a joint agreement -- well, he said it would be easier for me to pass through check-points set up by the BH Army if I had a document of this kind, and as we worked together over there, the business in Jablanica and so on and because I travelled to Konjic, he said, "Give me your photograph, and I'll make you a card saying you're a member of the BH Army," and that was in 1992. October 1992 when the conflict in Rama took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we've had a close look at this card. This could be twofold. Either we consider you're a general from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that case, Mr. Izetbegovic should appoint you officially. Or the second alternative is that General Pasalic gives you this so that you can go through the check-points, so that you have no problem there. Is it the first alternative or the second? Third maybe even.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second one, Judge Antonetti, and let me repeat again. I was not an HVO general, ever, never officially. Mate Boban, or whoever else -- well, I signed myself general because I was a general of the Croatian army. Unfortunately, that was the kind of war it was. Even if they persisted in trying to introduce law and order, the kind of law and order that exists in the West, nothing of the kind exists where we were. For a start, the HVO didn't have any ranks for a long time. The zone commander was referred to as the zone commander. He was called the zone commander. And it was only in 1993 -- Mr. Stojic knows this very well because this comes under his remit, but in July and August of 1993, the first ranks were assigned in the HVO. People would just be called brigade commander or Chief of the Main Staff, without ranks. No ranks were assigned until that time. Now, to lend me a bit of impetus, general from Croatia has arrived, you see, so I would write down "general" because it meant that I would achieve a little more of what I had been doing previously. But I wasn't a general of the BH Army or of the HVO, the Croatian Defence council. I was not a general of either of those two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, open the document, please, P01739 is the number. It is the presidential minutes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why don't we go through the documents 3D01228, for instance? Why don't we do that one?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 17th of January, 1993, signed by Enver Hadzihasanovic and Merdan Dzemal, and it relates to the commission for negotiations and the resolving the conflict in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You've already said --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the document -- or rather, on the 17th, they went to attend the meeting, Miro Andric and Zeljko Siljeg, they went. Well, it said that they had had consultations with me. That's what Enver Hadzihasanovic notes, because they told him that and they told him why I had gone down there. Probably they didn't tell him who had sent me, because I didn't say it out loud. But anyway, I want to tell you what was being offered at that time. But the HVO on the organisation of provinces was a temporary decision, a provisional decision based on reciprocity. That's what it says. So that can't be more logical than it is there, and then it says if there are changes in the final agreement in Geneva, the Croats will abide by them. So whatever the political leadership in Geneva decides the HVO army will abide by those agreements and decisions. Furthermore, it says that the HVO forces explicitly demand that the armed forces be withdrawn from the villages and that all units be returned to places from which they set out. And this refers to Jajce, because Gornji Vakuf wasn't under threat from the Army of Republika Srpska. So it's not clear why the areas under threat that is to say Tuzla, Zenica, threatened by the Serbs, why from those areas a brigade is being brought into Gornji Vakuf in addition to the brigade of the BH Army and is doing nothing to boot because the area that they covered was Raduski Kamen is a very small area. So people are walking around town bearing weapons, and it's just a matter of time when unrest would break out because soldiers who are not in the barracks or walking around bars in town with weapons, so it was only a question of days when a spark would ignite. It wasn't a matter or whether there would be unrest but only when there would be a disruption, unrest. Furthermore, the HVO guarantees that it would not do anything against Muslims who did not commit more crimes, so Paraga and that's what that deals with. Then it says that equality would be respected in all areas. But in the provinces, the number one man would have to be from the HVO and then the number two man would, of course, be from the BH Army and the principle of reciprocity would be applied and respected. Furthermore, that the trenches would be abandoned, especially the repeater, and the repeaters were I showed you pictures of those trenches here which meant absolute control over the roads in Gornji Vakuf and the surrounding areas and the trenches there resembled the kind of trenches that you had during World War I. Furthermore, a control of the army and commander and influence can no longer be exerted through Copcic [phoen], Agic, and Prijic because these were people who were Muslim extremists and were not in the army at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just draw -- draw the attention to a problem in the transcript. It's just disappeared. On page 92, line 21, it -- Mr. Praljak said that the army had the -- the HVO had requested to withdraw the army from the villages, but I read that the army should be taken towards the villages. That would be the opposite. Which was it? Do you recall, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were BH Army units which were composed of the population of Gornji Vakuf. So those people who made up the brigade of the BH Army from Gornji Vakuf, they would go to the villages from which they had come. They won't be on the hills that I mentioned. Now, the unit from Jajce, the brigade from Jajce, the Jajce Brigade, I think it was the one -- 307th or whatever the number of the brigade was, that one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Let's not get into numbers and stuff. What it says here that you said, line 20 of page 92, furthermore it says that the HVO forces explicitly demand that the armed forces be withdrawn from the villages, and in the text I read the HVO forces explicitly demand that the armed forces withdraw units towards the villages. Towards and from is the opposite. Which one is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards. Yes, towards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the villages. To go to the villages from which those people in the brigade were from originally. So when they weren't in town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. The error is corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll stop for now because it's just about 7.00 p.m. I'm sure we'll have ample opportunity to discuss this document tomorrow again. As you know, this week we shall also be sitting in the morning. Therefore, we shall reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. I wish you a pleasant evening.
